q:
Read the passage.

Telehealth visits grew quickly when many clinics closed their waiting rooms in 2020. Patients who had never used video calls learned to meet their doctors through a phone screen, and many clinics kept offering the option after reopening.

Not every visit works well on a screen, however. A clinician cannot listen to a patient's lungs, feel a swollen joint, or draw blood through a video link. Patients without reliable internet or a private place to talk may struggle to take part. For these reasons, many clinics now use video for follow-up visits and medication checks while asking patients to come in person for new symptoms and physical exams.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the second paragraph?
o: Clinicians cannot examine joints, listen to lungs or draw blood over a video link.
Patients without reliable internet access are unable to take part in telehealth visits.
Telehealth grew rapidly in 2020 and remained common after clinics reopened their doors.
Video visits have limits, so clinics match in-person and video care to the type of visit.
w: The second paragraph opens with its topic sentence (not every visit works well on a screen), lists the limits, and ends with the result: clinics use video for some visits and in-person care for others. This option captures both the limits and the response.

n.0: Too narrow: these physical limits are supporting details for the paragraph's point, not the point itself.
n.1: Distortion of one detail: the passage says such patients may struggle, not that they are unable to take part.
n.2: Wrong part of the passage: this is the main idea of the first paragraph, not the second.

q:
Read the passage.

Many people believe that food dropped on the floor is safe to eat if it is picked up within five seconds. Researchers who tested this idea dropped several foods, including watermelon, bread and gummy candy, onto surfaces coated with harmless bacteria. Bacteria reached some foods in less than one second. Time on the floor did matter, since longer contact transferred more bacteria, but the type of food mattered more. Wet watermelon picked up the most bacteria, while gummy candy picked up the least. The surface mattered too: carpet passed fewer bacteria to food than tile or stainless steel did. Speed, it turns out, is a poor guide to whether dropped food is clean.

Which title best fits the passage?
o: Testing the Five-Second Rule
How Bacteria Spread Through the Home
The Five-Second Rule Holds Up in the Lab
Watermelon: The Riskiest Food to Drop
w: A good title names the topic and fits the whole passage. The passage describes an experiment that tested the five-second belief and concludes that speed is a poor guide, so "Testing the Five-Second Rule" covers the entire text.

n.1: Too broad: the passage covers transfer from a floor surface to dropped food, not bacteria throughout a home.
n.2: Opposite of the passage: bacteria transferred in under one second, so the rule did not hold up.
n.3: Too narrow: watermelon is one result within the experiment, not the subject of the whole passage.

q:
Read the paragraph.

(1) Have you ever noticed that a scrape on your face seems to heal faster than one on your shin? (2) The speed at which a wound heals depends largely on its blood supply. (3) Blood delivers the oxygen and nutrients that new tissue needs in order to grow. (4) The face and scalp have an especially rich network of small vessels, so wounds there often close within days. (5) The lower legs, farther from the heart, tend to heal more slowly. (6) Conditions that narrow blood vessels, such as smoking, can slow healing anywhere on the body.

Which sentence is the topic sentence of the paragraph?
o: Sentence 6
Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
w: Sentence 2 states the paragraph's central claim (healing speed depends on blood supply). Sentences 3 to 6 explain why and give examples: what blood delivers, fast healing in the face, slow healing in the legs, and narrowed vessels.

n.0: Sentence 6 is a final example of the same idea; a last sentence is not automatically the topic sentence.
n.1: Sentence 1 is a hook question that draws the reader in; it raises the topic but makes no claim.
n.3: Sentence 3 explains why blood supply matters, so it supports the topic sentence rather than stating it.

q:
Read the passage.

In a growing number of counties, paramedics spend part of their shifts visiting patients at home rather than waiting for emergency calls. These community paramedicine programs focus on people who call 911 often or who were recently discharged from the hospital. During a visit, a paramedic may check blood pressure, review a patient's medicine bottles for duplicates, and look for hazards such as loose rugs. One county program reported that frequent callers enrolled for six months made about half as many 911 calls as before. Programs are often funded by grants, and some counties have struggled to keep them running when the grants end. Even so, supporters see home visits as a way to treat small problems before they become emergencies.

The main idea of the passage is that community paramedicine programs use home visits to head off emergencies. Which details from the passage support this main idea? Select all that apply.
o: Paramedics review patients' medicine bottles for duplicates.
Paramedics check patients' homes for hazards such as loose rugs.
Enrolled frequent callers made about half as many 911 calls.
Some counties have struggled to keep their programs running.
Paramedics visit patients in the hospital before discharge.
Programs are often paid for with grants that can run out.
w: A supporting detail shows how or that home visits prevent emergencies. Checking for duplicate medicines and for fall hazards are preventive actions, and the drop in 911 calls is evidence that the visits head off emergencies.

n.3: Struggling to keep programs running is a drawback the author concedes, not support for the main idea.
n.4: Distortion: the passage describes home visits to people already discharged, not hospital visits before discharge.
n.5: Grant funding is about how programs are paid for, a limitation rather than support for the idea that visits prevent emergencies.

q:
Read the passage.

Older adults who volunteer regularly tend to report better health than those who do not. In several long-term studies, retirees who volunteered a few hours a week were less likely to develop high blood pressure and more likely to stay physically active. Researchers think the benefits come partly from staying busy and partly from social contact, since loneliness is linked to poorer health in later life. Volunteering also gives many retirees a sense of purpose that paid work once provided. The studies cannot fully rule out that healthier people are simply more likely to volunteer in the first place. Even with that caution, the pattern has encouraged some senior centers to connect members with local charities.

Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Loneliness in later life is linked to poorer health among retired adults.
Senior centers should require their members to volunteer with local charities.
Older adults who volunteer tend to be healthier, likely because of activity, contact and purpose.
Researchers cannot yet tell whether volunteering improves health or healthy people volunteer more.
w: Most of the passage describes the link between volunteering and better health in older adults and the likely reasons (staying busy, social contact, purpose). The caution about healthier people volunteering is one qualifying sentence, so the main idea keeps the emphasis on the health link.

n.0: Too narrow: the loneliness link is offered as one explanation for the benefits, not as the central point.
n.1: Distortion: senior centers connect members with charities; the passage never says they should require volunteering.
n.3: Reversed emphasis: the caution is a single qualifying sentence, and the author says the pattern holds "even with that caution."

q:
Read the passage.

Many people assume that a fever is the illness itself and must be brought down right away. In fact, a fever is one of the body's defenses. When the immune system detects an infection, it signals the brain to raise the body's temperature set point. Many bacteria and viruses reproduce less efficiently at higher temperatures, and some immune cells work faster when the body is warmer. For most healthy adults, a moderate fever is uncomfortable but not dangerous. Doctors still advise seeking care for a very high fever, a fever that lasts several days, or any fever in a young infant, because in those cases the underlying cause may need treatment.

Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: A fever that lasts several days or occurs in an infant may need a doctor's care.
Some immune cells work faster when the body's temperature rises during illness.
People should bring a fever down quickly to keep an infection from spreading.
A fever is often a helpful defense against infection, not simply an illness to stop.
w: The passage opens with a common belief and then corrects it with "In fact, a fever is one of the body's defenses." The rest explains how the fever helps fight infection, with a closing note about when to seek care. The correction is the main idea.

n.0: Too narrow: the closing advice about when to seek care qualifies the main idea rather than stating it.
n.1: Too narrow: faster immune cells are one detail explaining why fever is a defense.
n.2: This is the belief the author sets up in order to correct it, not the author's own point.

q:
Read the paragraph.

(1) Children who go to bed at the same time each night tend to fall asleep faster. (2) A steady bedtime helps set the body's internal clock, which controls when a child begins to feel drowsy. (3) Researchers have linked regular bedtimes to better attention and behavior in school. (4) Teenagers' internal clocks shift later, which is why many feel alert late at night. (5) Even on weekends, keeping bedtime within an hour of the weekday time helps the clock stay steady. (6) Families that build a short routine, such as a bath, a book and lights out, often find that bedtime battles become less frequent.

The main idea of the paragraph is that a consistent bedtime benefits children. Which sentence does NOT support this main idea?
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
Sentence 5
w: Sentence 4 shares a key phrase (internal clock) with the paragraph, but it describes a natural shift in teenagers' clocks, not a benefit of a consistent bedtime for children. The other listed sentences each explain, show or extend that benefit.

n.0: Sentence 3 gives evidence of a benefit: better attention and behavior in school.
n.2: Sentence 2 explains how a steady bedtime helps, by setting the internal clock that controls drowsiness.
n.3: Sentence 5 explains how to keep the benefit on weekends, so it supports the idea of a consistent bedtime.

q:
Read the passage.

When Lorraine Whitfield finished nursing school in 1971, the nearest hospital to her hometown in rural Mississippi was a ninety-minute drive away. She spent her first years working night shifts in the city and driving home on weekends to check on neighbors who had no doctor. In 1978 she persuaded a church congregation to donate an old school bus, which she and two volunteers fitted with an exam table, a refrigerator for vaccines and a folding ramp. For the next twenty years, the bus visited eleven towns on a fixed weekly route. By the time Whitfield retired, the county had opened two permanent clinics, both built at stops where the bus had drawn the longest lines.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Lorraine Whitfield worked night shifts in a city hospital before moving back to rural Mississippi.
Rural Mississippi counties needed more hospitals in the 1970s than the state's cities did.
Lorraine Whitfield brought regular care to underserved towns, which helped lead to permanent clinics.
A church donated a school bus that volunteers turned into a mobile clinic in 1978.
w: The passage follows Whitfield from seeing the lack of nearby care, to building a mobile clinic, to twenty years of weekly visits, to permanent clinics built at the busiest stops. The main idea links her work to that lasting result.

n.0: Distortion and too narrow: she drove home on weekends, and the passage never says she moved back; this is also only an early detail.
n.1: Too broad and outside the passage: it never compares how many hospitals cities and rural counties needed.
n.3: Too narrow: the donated bus is one event in the story, not the point the whole passage makes.

q:
Read the passage.

Teachers at Lincoln Middle School noticed that many students arrived tired and unfocused, and a survey found that about a third had eaten nothing before school. The cafeteria served a free breakfast, but it closed when the first bell rang, and students who came on late buses missed it.

Last fall the school tried a different approach. Carts of breakfast items were delivered to homerooms, and students ate during the first ten minutes of class while teachers took attendance. Within a month, the share of students eating school breakfast rose from 28 percent to 71 percent.

Some teachers had worried about spills and lost class time. After the first semester, most said the routine ran smoothly, and the school nurse reported fewer morning visits from students complaining of headaches or stomachaches.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: About a third of the students at Lincoln Middle School skipped breakfast at home, which left many of them tired and unfocused.
After many students skipped breakfast, the school began serving it in homerooms, which raised participation and mostly ran smoothly.
Breakfast participation at Lincoln Middle School rose from 28 percent to 71 percent within one month of the change.
Lincoln's homeroom breakfast raised students' focus and test scores, so nearby schools have begun to copy it.
w: A summary covers every paragraph in order: the problem (students skipping breakfast because the cafeteria closed at the bell), the solution (breakfast in homerooms) and the results (participation rose, worries mostly did not come true). Only this option includes all three.

n.0: Summarizes only the first paragraph; it leaves out the change the school made and its results.
n.2: Too narrow: the participation figures are one supporting detail from the second paragraph.
n.3: Goes beyond the passage: it never measures focus or test scores, and it never mentions other schools copying the plan.

q:
Read the passage.

Standing desks have become a common sight in offices, promoted as a cure for the health risks of sitting all day. Long periods of sitting are linked to back pain, weight gain and heart disease, so the appeal is easy to understand.

Standing all day, however, brings its own problems. Workers who stand for most of a shift report more leg swelling, foot pain and varicose veins than those who sit. A standing worker also burns only slightly more energy than a seated one, far too little to replace exercise.

Researchers who study workplace health now suggest a middle path: change positions often, take short walking breaks, and treat the desk as one tool among several rather than a solution in itself.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Standing desks are popular, but standing all day has its own costs, so experts advise shifting positions and moving often.
Standing burns only slightly more energy than sitting, so workers who use standing desks still need regular exercise.
Standing desks harm workers by causing leg swelling and foot pain, so offices should stop buying them for employees.
Sitting for long periods is linked to back pain, weight gain and heart disease, which explains why standing desks are popular.
w: The passage moves from the appeal of standing desks (paragraph 1), to the problems of standing all day (paragraph 2), to the recommended middle path (paragraph 3). This option keeps all three points in the same order and adds no opinion.

n.1: Too narrow: the energy comparison is one detail in the second paragraph.
n.2: Distortion with an added recommendation: the researchers suggest treating the desk as one tool among several, not that offices stop buying them.
n.3: Summarizes only the first paragraph and leaves out the problems with standing and the advice that follows.

q:
Read the passage.

In April, the city of Fairview painted protected bike lanes on six blocks of Main Street, replacing a row of parking spaces. The pilot was scheduled to run for six months.

During the pilot, the number of cyclists counted on Main Street each weekday doubled, and the city recorded no bicycle crashes on those blocks, compared with four in the same months of the previous year. Several shop owners said that losing parking had cut into their sales, although city sales-tax records showed little change for the area.

The city council will vote in November on whether to make the lanes permanent.

Which summary of the passage is the most objective?
o: Fairview's bike lane pilot doubled cycling with no crashes; some shops reported lost sales, and a council vote is pending.
Fairview's bike lanes hurt Main Street shops by removing parking, in exchange for a modest rise in the number of cyclists.
Fairview's successful bike lane pilot doubled cycling and ended crashes on Main Street, so the council should keep the lanes.
Fairview's bike lane pilot was so popular with cyclists that the council has decided to make the Main Street lanes permanent.
w: An objective summary restates the main points without taking sides or adding information. This option reports the results, the shop owners' complaint and the pending vote, all as the passage presents them.

n.1: Slanted: it presents the shop owners' claim as fact, though tax records showed little change, and calls a doubling "modest."
n.2: Adds the writer's judgment ("successful," "should keep the lanes"), which makes the summary an opinion.
n.3: Inaccurate: the council has not decided anything; the passage says the vote will happen in November.

q:
Read the passage.

Hospitals are noisier than most people expect. Alarms from monitors and pumps, overhead pages, rolling carts and conversations at nursing stations can push nighttime sound levels well above what sleep researchers recommend for bedrooms.

The noise matters because sleep is part of recovery. Patients who sleep poorly in the hospital often report more pain and more confusion, and they may be slower to regain strength. Staff are affected as well: frequent alarms that turn out to be harmless can lead nurses to respond more slowly to the ones that count.

Some hospitals have tried quiet hours, softer flooring and alarms that alert only the assigned nurse's phone. A few units report better patient sleep scores, although the changes can be costly to install.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Changes such as softer flooring and phone-based alarms are costly for hospitals to install on their units.
Frequent harmless alarms can lead nurses to respond more slowly to the alarms that signal real problems.
Hospitals are noisier than people expect because of monitors, pages, carts and conversations at stations.
Hospital noise disrupts patient sleep and staff response, and some hospitals are testing ways to reduce it.
w: Paragraph 1 describes the noise, paragraph 2 explains why it matters for patients and staff, and paragraph 3 describes efforts to reduce it. This option combines all three with the same emphasis as the passage.

n.0: Reversed emphasis: the cost of the changes is a brief qualification at the very end, not the passage's central point.
n.1: Too narrow: alarm fatigue is one detail in the second paragraph.
n.2: Summarizes only the first paragraph and leaves out why the noise matters and what hospitals are doing.

q:
Read the original passage and a student's version of it.

Original passage: Although the vaccine is given in two doses spaced a few months apart, many adults who receive the first dose do not return for the second. In one health system, about 60 percent of patients completed the series. When the system began sending text reminders a week before the second dose was due, completion rose to about 80 percent. Patients who received a reminder that included a link to book online were the most likely to return.

Student's version: Many adults skip the second dose of a two-dose vaccine, but reminder texts, especially ones with an online booking link, helped one health system raise completion from about 60 to 80 percent.

Which statement best describes the student's version?
o: It is a summary, because it condenses the main point and key support into fewer words.
It is a paraphrase, because it shifts the original's main point to the booking link.
It is a paraphrase, because it restates the original passage at about the same length.
It is a summary, because it adds the student's own view of why patients skip doses.
w: A summary restates the main idea and the most important support in the reader's own words and is shorter than the original. The student's single sentence keeps the problem, the solution and the result in far fewer words, so it is a summary.

n.1: The main point (reminders raised completion) is unchanged; the booking link appears as supporting detail, as in the original.
n.2: A paraphrase stays close to the original's length; the student's version is one sentence compared with four.
n.3: The student adds no personal view; an added opinion would make it a weaker summary, not define one.

q:
Read the passage and the student's summary.

Passage: Community fridges are refrigerators placed on sidewalks or outside businesses where anyone can leave or take food at any hour. Many appeared in U.S. cities in 2020, when job losses left more families short on groceries. Most are run by volunteers, who clean them, check dates and post rules, and local bakeries and grocers often donate unsold food. Organizers say the fridges succeed because they ask no questions; people who feel embarrassed to visit a food pantry can take what they need without signing a form. Keeping the fridges clean and stocked, however, depends on a steady supply of volunteers.

Student's summary: (1) Community fridges are public refrigerators where anyone can leave or take food at any time. (2) Volunteers keep them clean, and stores donate unsold food. (3) Their no-questions approach is the best way to fight hunger in America. (4) Their success depends on a steady supply of volunteers.

Which sentence should be removed from the student's summary?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 3
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
w: A summary must be objective and add nothing new. The passage reports that organizers credit the no-questions approach for the fridges' success; it never claims this is the best way to fight hunger nationwide. Sentence 3 adds the student's own judgment.

n.0: Sentence 1 accurately restates the opening definition, which a summary needs.
n.2: Sentence 2 condenses the key point about how the fridges are run and supplied.
n.3: Sentence 4 restates the passage's closing point about the fridges' reliance on volunteers.

q:
Read the passage.

Last summer, the town of Mesa Verde faced its driest season in forty years, and its reservoir fell to 30 percent of capacity. The water district asked residents to cut their use by one fifth.

The district paired the request with practical help. It offered rebates of up to $500 for replacing lawns with native plants, gave away low-flow showerheads, and posted each neighborhood's weekly water use on its website. Mayor Tina Okafor, who had replaced her own lawn with cactus and gravel, appeared in a video about the rebates.

By September, total water use had fallen 23 percent from the year before. District officials credit the neighborhood reports most of all, saying residents responded when they could compare their use with their neighbors'.

Which statements belong in a summary of the passage? Select all that apply.
o: Other towns facing a severe drought should post each neighborhood's weekly water use online.
Water use fell 23 percent, a drop officials credit mainly to the neighborhood reports.
Residents cut back mainly because $500 rebates covered the full cost of replacing a lawn.
During a severe drought, the water district asked residents to cut their use by one fifth.
Mayor Tina Okafor replaced her own lawn with cactus and gravel before appearing in a rebate video.
The district backed its request with rebates, free fixtures and neighborhood use reports.
w: A summary keeps each paragraph's key point in order: the drought and the request (paragraph 1), the district's support measures (paragraph 2), and the result with the officials' explanation (paragraph 3).

n.0: This is a recommendation the passage never makes; a summary adds no opinions.
n.2: Distortion: rebates were up to $500, the passage never says they covered the full cost, and officials credit the reports, not the rebates, most.
n.4: The mayor's own lawn is a minor detail; a summary leaves out such details.

q:
Read the passage.

Marcus had rehearsed his speech for the scholarship committee a dozen times in front of the bathroom mirror. When he walked into the room, though, the five faces at the long table made his notes feel like someone else's words. He stumbled through the first paragraph, then stopped. For a long moment he said nothing. Then he folded the paper and told them about the winter his grandmother was sick, when he had learned to check her blood sugar and cook her meals before school, and how that winter had made him want to become a nurse. When he finished, one committee member was writing quickly, and another nodded. Outside, Marcus realized he could not remember a single line of the speech he had practiced.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: One winter Marcus cared for his sick grandmother before school, which made him want to become a nurse.
Nervous, Marcus abandoned his rehearsed speech and spoke from experience, which seemed to engage the panel.
Marcus won a nursing scholarship after he told the committee a moving story about his grandmother.
Marcus practiced a scholarship speech many times but forgot most of it when he faced the committee.
w: The passage moves from Marcus's preparation, to his loss of confidence, to his decision to speak from personal experience, to the committee's positive reaction. This option covers that whole arc without adding events.

n.0: This is the backstory Marcus tells, a detail inside the story rather than a summary of the passage.
n.2: Goes beyond the text: the committee seemed engaged, but the passage never says Marcus won the scholarship.
n.3: Covers only the first part of the story and leaves out what Marcus did instead and how the committee responded.

q:
Read the passage.

A first-time blood donor often expects the process to take a few minutes, but a whole visit usually lasts about an hour. It begins with registration, where the donor shows identification and reads information about who should not give blood.

Next comes a brief health screening in a private area. A staff member checks the donor's temperature, pulse and blood pressure and pricks a finger to make sure the donor's iron level is high enough. Only then does the donation itself begin, and it takes roughly ten minutes to collect about a pint.

Afterward, donors rest for about fifteen minutes and have a snack and a drink, which helps prevent dizziness before they leave.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Staff check each donor's temperature, pulse, blood pressure and iron level before the donation starts.
The donation itself takes about ten minutes and collects roughly one pint of blood from the donor.
Most first-time donors feel dizzy after giving blood, so they must rest and eat before they leave.
Giving blood takes about an hour: registration, a health screening, a short donation and a brief rest.
w: The passage states that a visit lasts about an hour and then walks through its stages in order: registration, screening, donation and rest. This option captures the main point and every stage in sequence.

n.0: Too narrow: the screening checks are details of a single stage.
n.1: Too narrow: the length of the draw is one detail from the second paragraph.
n.2: Distortion: the rest and snack help prevent dizziness; the passage never says most donors feel dizzy.

q:
Read the passage.

For most of the twentieth century, the Harlan textile mill employed nearly half the working adults in Pine Ridge. When the mill closed in 1998, hundreds of families moved away to find work, and the town's population dropped by a third within five years.

With fewer children enrolled, the district merged Pine Ridge's two elementary schools into one. The empty building sat unused until 2015, when a group of residents raised money to turn it into a community health center.

Today the center employs forty people, and its staff includes several former students of the old school.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Pine Ridge lost a third of its people after the district merged its two elementary schools, which led the mill to close.
Residents of Pine Ridge raised money in 2015 to build a new community health center that now employs forty people.
After the mill closed and families left, Pine Ridge merged its schools, and residents turned the empty one into a clinic.
The Harlan textile mill employed nearly half of Pine Ridge's working adults for most of the twentieth century.
w: The passage is a chain of causes and effects: the mill closed, families left, enrollment fell, the schools merged, and residents later turned the empty school into a health center. This option keeps that chain in the correct order.

n.0: Reverses cause and effect: the mill closing caused the population loss, which led to the school merger, not the other way around.
n.1: Distortion: residents converted the old school building rather than building a new center, and the option skips the cause.
n.3: Too narrow: this is background from the first sentence only.

q:
Read the passage.

Emergency departments in many hospitals are crowded not because too many patients arrive, but because admitted patients cannot leave. When the hospital's inpatient beds are full, people who have already been admitted wait in the emergency department, sometimes for a day or more. Their stretchers fill hallways and slow care for new arrivals.

Mercy General tackled the problem by changing its discharge routine. Instead of sending most recovered patients home in the late afternoon, units now aim to complete discharges before 11 a.m., and a team of transport aides helps patients who are waiting for rides. Within a year, the average time admitted patients spent waiting in the emergency department fell from nine hours to four.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Patients who wait in emergency department hallways for a day or more receive slower and less safe care.
Emergency departments are crowded because too many patients come in with minor problems that belong elsewhere.
Admitted patients waiting for beds crowd emergency rooms, and Mercy General cut waits by discharging earlier.
Mercy General hired a team of transport aides to help discharged patients who were waiting for rides home.
w: The passage is organized as a problem (admitted patients stuck in the emergency department because beds are full) and a solution (earlier discharges at Mercy General, which cut waits). A summary should state both.

n.0: Distortion: the passage says hallway stretchers slow care for new arrivals; it does not say waiting patients get less safe care.
n.1: Opposite of the passage: the author says crowding is not caused by too many arrivals.
n.3: Too narrow: the transport aides are one part of the solution.

q:
Read the passage.

Until the late 1960s, a person in the United States who needed help in an emergency had to know the local number for the police, the fire department or an ambulance service, and those numbers differed from town to town. Callers who did not know the right number often dialed the operator, who then had to find and connect the correct agency.

In 1967, a presidential commission recommended a single number for reporting emergencies nationwide. The telephone company chose 911 because it was short, easy to remember and not already used as an area code or exchange. The first 911 call was placed in Haleyville, Alabama, in February 1968.

Adoption was slow, since each community had to build its own call center, but by the end of the century most Americans could reach help by dialing the same three digits.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: To replace confusing local numbers, 911 became a single emergency number that spread slowly nationwide.
Before the late 1960s, callers had to know a different local emergency number or rely on an operator.
Because a 1967 commission chose 911, Haleyville, Alabama, built the nation's first emergency call center.
The phone company picked 911 because it was short, easy to remember and not used as an area code.
w: The passage describes the problem (many local numbers), the solution (a single number, 911, first used in 1968) and the outcome (slow adoption, then nationwide reach). This option includes all three in order.

n.1: Summarizes only the first paragraph, the problem, and leaves out the solution and its spread.
n.2: Distortion: the passage says the telephone company chose 911 and that the first call was placed in Haleyville; it never says Haleyville built the first call center.
n.3: Too narrow: the reasons for choosing 911 are a supporting detail in the second paragraph.

q:
Read the passage.

Dana checked the clock above the nurses' station for the third time in ten minutes. Her coffee had gone cold beside a stack of charts she had not opened. When the elevator chimed, she turned so quickly that her pen rolled off the counter, and when a man with a delivery cart stepped out instead of her daughter's surgeon, she sat back down and pressed her palms flat against the desk. A coworker offered to cover her patients for an hour. Dana shook her head. "I need something to do," she said, and opened the top chart.

Which of the following can the reader infer about Dana?
o: She is expecting a delivery of supplies that she ordered for her unit.
She is irritated that her coworker doubts her ability to work.
She is anxiously waiting for news about her daughter's surgery.
She has fallen behind on her charting because she is new to the unit.
w: Several clues combine: she keeps checking the clock, she spins toward the elevator, she slumps when someone other than her daughter's surgeon steps out, and she wants work to keep busy. Together they support anxious waiting for news about the surgery.

n.0: Misreads the scene: she sits back down when the delivery cart appears, showing it is not what she was waiting for.
n.1: Nothing suggests irritation; she declines the offer because she wants something to do, not because she feels doubted.
n.3: The unopened charts reflect distraction; nothing in the passage says she is new or behind for that reason.

q:
Read the leaflet.

Your Child's First Visit to the Dentist
Bring along a favorite toy or blanket so your child has something familiar to hold. At the visit, the hygienist will count your child's teeth with a small mirror; we call it the "tooth parade." At home, avoid words like hurt, shot or drill, which can make a young child anxious before the appointment even begins. Afterward, praise your child for being brave, even if there were a few tears. Before you leave, schedule the next checkup; most children need one every six months. Questions? Call our front desk.

The leaflet is most likely written for which audience?
o: Dental hygienists learning to work with nervous young patients
Young children preparing for their first dental cleaning
Parents of teenagers who feel anxious about dental work
Parents of young children seeing a dentist for the first time
w: The leaflet addresses "you" about "your child," tells the reader what to bring, what to say at home and what to schedule, and mentions toys, blankets and a playful "tooth parade." These clues point to parents of young children before a first visit.

n.0: The reader is told what the hygienist will do, so the reader is not the hygienist.
n.1: The child is referred to as "your child," so the reader is the adult, not the child.
n.2: Toys, blankets, a "tooth parade" and a first visit point to young children, not teenagers.

q:
Read the passage.

In the 1840s, a Vienna hospital ran two maternity wards. In one, women were delivered by doctors and medical students; in the other, by midwives. Mothers in the doctors' ward died of fever far more often, and some women begged to be admitted to the midwives' ward instead. The physician Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that the doctors often came straight from performing autopsies. When he required them to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients, deaths in their ward fell sharply. Many of his colleagues rejected his findings, partly because germs had not yet been identified as a cause of disease.

Why does the author most likely mention that some women begged to be admitted to the midwives' ward?
o: To suggest that the midwives in Vienna were better trained than the doctors
To explain why Semmelweis began requiring the doctors to wash their hands
To illustrate why Semmelweis's colleagues rejected his findings about fever
To show that the gap in death rates was so large that even patients knew of it
w: The detail comes right after the statement that mothers in the doctors' ward died far more often. Women pleading to avoid that ward shows the difference was obvious and well known, which makes the problem vivid for the reader.

n.0: The passage never compares training; it links the deaths to doctors coming from autopsies.
n.1: The handwashing rule is explained by the autopsy observation, not by the women's requests.
n.2: Wrong part of the passage: the colleagues' rejection is explained by germs not yet being identified.

q:
Read the passage.

The Garcias' tomato plants grew tall and green all summer but produced only a handful of fruit. Their neighbor, whose garden got the same sun and water, harvested baskets of tomatoes from the same variety. Mrs. Garcia had fed her plants a high-nitrogen fertilizer every week, while the neighbor fertilized once in the spring. A worker at the garden center explained that nitrogen encourages leaves and stems, and that too much of it can lead a plant to put its energy into foliage instead of fruit.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: The Garcias' plants most likely produced little fruit because they received too much nitrogen.
The Garcias' plants produced little fruit because they were a less productive tomato variety.
Feeding the plants high-nitrogen fertilizer more often would have increased the Garcias' harvest.
The neighbor's garden received more sunlight, which helped the tomatoes ripen more quickly.
w: The passage rules out the other differences (same sun, water and variety) and leaves one: weekly high-nitrogen feeding versus a single spring feeding. Combined with the explanation that too much nitrogen favors leaves over fruit, excess nitrogen is the best-supported cause.

n.1: Contradicted: both gardens grew the same variety.
n.2: Opposite of the passage: too much nitrogen pushes the plant's energy into leaves, so more frequent feeding would make the problem worse.
n.3: Contradicted: the gardens got the same sun and water.

q:
Read the memo.

To: All Third-Floor Staff
From: Janet Liu, Nurse Manager
Date: March 3
Subject: Supply room

Starting Monday, the third-floor supply room will be locked at all times, and staff will badge in to enter. Each item removed must be scanned at the new station by the door. Please do not prop the door open, even during busy shifts. Last month's inventory showed that we were billed for far more wound-care supplies than were charted for patients. Thank you for helping us keep costs under control.

Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the memo?
o: The manager believes supplies have been leaving the room without being recorded.
The supply room was previously locked during night shifts but not day shifts.
The hospital plans to stop stocking wound-care supplies on the third floor.
Staff members have been taking wound-care supplies home for their own use.
w: The memo pairs new controls (locking, badging, scanning each item) with a gap between supplies billed and supplies charted. The most reasonable inference is that the manager thinks items are being removed without a record.

n.1: Unsupported: the memo says nothing about the room's earlier locking schedule.
n.2: Unsupported: the memo changes how supplies are accessed, not whether they are stocked.
n.3: Overreaches: unrecorded use could come from charting errors or waste; the memo never accuses anyone of taking supplies home.

q:
Read the passage.

By the third week of flu season, the clinic's waiting room had become a tide that never went out. Patients filled every chair by eight in the morning, and by noon a line stretched past the pharmacy window. The receptionists stopped looking up from their screens. Dr. Patel ate lunch standing in the supply closet, and the nurses traded their usual jokes for quick nods. Still, every patient who came through the door was seen before the clinic closed, even when that meant locking up after nine at night.

The phrase "a tide that never went out" suggests that the waiting room
o: stayed full as new patients kept arriving throughout the day
emptied each afternoon after the busy morning rush ended
was busiest during the hours after the clinic had closed
was flooded during a storm that delayed patients' visits
w: A tide that never goes out stays high. The details that follow (chairs full by eight, a line by noon, staff working past nine) confirm the room stayed crowded as patients kept coming all day.

n.1: Opposite of the metaphor: the tide never went out, and the line grew by noon.
n.2: Misreads the detail about locking up late, which shows staff stayed to finish, not that the room was busiest after closing.
n.3: Takes the metaphor literally; nothing in the passage describes water or a storm.

q:
Read the passage.

When our clinic switched to an online patient portal last spring, I expected to miss the phone calls. Instead, I found I could read my test results the day they came back, message my doctor at midnight without feeling like a bother, and refill a prescription in less time than it takes to brew coffee. My father, who is eighty-one, still prefers to call, and the clinic has kept a phone line for patients like him. I do wish the portal's menus were simpler; finding an old message can take five clicks. Those are small complaints, though, next to the hours I no longer spend on hold.

Which best describes the author's attitude toward the patient portal?
o: Reluctant acceptance of a change the author did not want
Mostly favorable, with a few minor reservations
Strong criticism of the portal's confusing menu design
Concern that the portal shuts out older patients
w: The author lists several benefits, mentions one complaint about the menus, and then calls it a "small complaint" compared with the time saved. That is a mostly positive attitude with minor reservations.

n.0: The author expected to miss phone calls, but the word "Instead" signals that the portal turned out better than expected.
n.2: Overstates the one complaint, which the author explicitly calls small.
n.3: The clinic kept a phone line for older patients like the author's father, so the author does not raise this concern.

q:
Read the passage.

Ana's shift at the animal shelter began at six, but she arrived at five-thirty every Saturday so that she could walk Biscuit before the other volunteers came in. Biscuit, a gray pit bull mix, had lived at the shelter for fourteen months, longer than any other dog. Visitors usually walked past his kennel because he barked at strangers, and twice he had been returned by families who adopted him. With Ana, though, he sat for treats and walked calmly on his leash. One Saturday, Ana brought her roommate along and asked her to hold the leash. Biscuit sniffed the roommate's shoes, then sat. Ana smiled and took a photo for the shelter's website.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? Select all that apply.
o: Biscuit was returned twice because he bit a member of a family.
Ana has formed a close bond with Biscuit.
Biscuit is the oldest of the dogs currently living at the shelter.
Ana hopes to improve Biscuit's chances of being adopted.
Biscuit behaves better with familiar people than with strangers.
Ana's roommate is nervous around large dogs she has not met before.
w: Ana comes early every week to walk Biscuit, so they are close. He barks at strangers but is calm with Ana, so he is better with people he knows. Testing him with a new person and posting a calm photo on the shelter's website suggest she wants to help him find a home.

n.0: The passage says he was returned twice but never gives a reason; a bite is an assumption.
n.2: Distortion: Biscuit has been at the shelter the longest, which says nothing about his age.
n.5: Nothing describes the roommate's feelings; she simply holds the leash.

q:
Read the passage.

Grandpa Eli unfolded the paper map across the hood of the station wagon and traced the route with his finger. The nearest pay phone was back at the gas station, eleven miles behind them, and the last town had been too small for a motel. Ruthie, nine years old, rewound the tape in her cassette player with a pencil because the batteries had died somewhere in Nebraska. Her mother checked the cooler: four sandwiches, a jar of pickles and two warm sodas. "We'll make Cheyenne by dark," Grandpa said, though no one had seen a road sign in nearly an hour.

Based on details in the passage, when does the story most likely take place?
o: During the early years of the automobile, in the first decade of the 1900s
In a time before cell phones and digital music players were common
In the present day, on a road with no cell phone coverage
In midwinter, when snow often closes the roads in Nebraska
w: A paper map, a pay phone eleven miles back and a battery-powered cassette player point to a time after cassettes were common but before cell phones and digital music were. The family relies on a pay phone, not a phone they carry.

n.0: Cassette players and station wagons rule out the first decade of the 1900s.
n.2: A cassette player and a pay phone as the nearest phone point to the past, not the present day.
n.3: Nothing mentions snow or cold; the warm sodas, if anything, suggest the opposite.

q:
Read the passage.

The Westbrook Public Health Department offered free flu shots at three locations last October. The downtown clinic, open weekdays from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., gave 410 shots. A kiosk at the mall, open weekday evenings and all day on weekends, gave 1,280. A mobile van that parked outside large workplaces at lunchtime gave 960. This year the department has the same budget and staff, and it plans to close one of the three locations.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Many residents found it easier to get a shot outside standard weekday business hours.
Residents who live downtown were less worried about the flu than residents elsewhere.
Most residents would rather get a flu shot at work than at a clinic or a mall.
The department will close the mall kiosk because it costs the most to operate.
w: The location open evenings and weekends gave the most shots (1,280), more than three times the weekday-hours clinic (410). That pattern best supports the conclusion that many people found off-hours more convenient.

n.1: Unsupported: the downtown clinic's location and hours explain the lower number as well as any attitude; the passage says nothing about worry.
n.2: Overreaches: the workplace van gave fewer shots (960) than the mall kiosk, so "most residents" prefer work is not supported.
n.3: Unsupported: the passage gives no costs and does not say which location will close.

q:
Read the passage.

Each year, thousands of people in the United States wait for a kidney transplant, and many will wait more than three years.

Consider Ray Delgado, a 52-year-old bus driver from Tucson. Ray spends four hours at a dialysis center three mornings a week. He has given up his route, his weekend softball league and the road trips he once took with his grandchildren. "I'm alive," he says, "but I'm waiting to live."

A single living donor can end that wait. Most healthy adults can donate a kidney and lead normal lives afterward, and the donor's medical costs are generally covered. Anyone curious about donating can contact a transplant center for a free screening.

What is the most likely purpose of the second paragraph?
o: To give a personal example that makes the long wait feel real to readers
To present an opposing view on whether to become a living donor
To suggest that bus drivers face a higher risk of kidney disease
To explain the medical steps involved in kidney dialysis treatment
w: The first paragraph states a statistic about long waits. The second turns that number into one person's life: the hours on dialysis, the activities he gave up and his own words. The detail humanizes the problem before the final paragraph asks readers to consider donating.

n.1: Ray's story supports the case for donation; no opposing view appears in the passage.
n.2: Ray's job is a personal detail; the passage makes no claim about bus drivers' risk.
n.3: The paragraph mentions how long Ray spends at dialysis but never explains the treatment's steps.

q:
Read the passage.

For years I believed I was simply bad at math. In high school I copied formulas onto index cards, memorized them the night before tests, and forgot them by the following week. When I enrolled in a nursing prerequisite course at twenty-eight, the instructor, Ms. Reyes, refused to hand out formulas to memorize. Instead she made us work out dosage problems with real medicine labels and explain each step aloud to a partner. The first month was miserable. By the final exam, though, I could set up a problem I had never seen before, and I realized I could not remember the last time I had written a formula on a card.

Which conclusion about the narrator is best supported by the passage?
o: The narrator's earlier struggles came from memorizing rather than understanding.
The narrator still prefers to memorize formulas on index cards before a test.
The narrator went on to earn the highest score in the prerequisite course.
The narrator found the course easy from the start because of Ms. Reyes's methods.
w: The narrator once memorized and quickly forgot formulas and believed they were bad at math. After learning to reason through problems and explain each step, the narrator could solve unfamiliar problems. The contrast suggests the earlier trouble came from the study method, not a lack of ability.

n.1: Opposite of the passage: the narrator no longer writes formulas on cards.
n.2: Unsupported: the passage says the narrator could solve new problems, not how the narrator ranked.
n.3: Contradicted: the narrator says the first month was miserable.

q:
Read the passage.

After Brookside Hospital placed hand-sanitizer dispensers outside every patient room on its surgical unit, managers tracked how often staff cleaned their hands. Before the change, observers saw staff clean their hands at about half of the moments when they should have. Six months later, the rate had risen to about three quarters. Over the same period, the number of infections patients picked up on the unit fell by about a fifth. During those six months, the hospital also hired two infection-prevention nurses, who ran training sessions on every unit.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Hand cleaning rose after the change, though the dispensers may not be the sole reason for it.
The dispensers probably did more than the nurses' training to raise hand cleaning.
Infections on the unit fell by about three quarters, likely because hand cleaning improved.
The infection-prevention nurses, rather than the dispensers, caused the drop in infections.
w: The rate of hand cleaning clearly rose (from about half to about three quarters), but the new nurses' training happened during the same six months. The evidence supports the rise while leaving the cause uncertain, which is what this option says.

n.1: Unsupported: the dispensers and the training began in the same six months, and the passage gives no way to compare their effects.
n.2: Misreads the figures: infections fell by about a fifth; about three quarters is the new hand-cleaning rate.
n.3: Unsupported: the passage gives no way to separate the effect of the training from the effect of the dispensers.

q:
Read the passage.

A survey of 300 first-year nursing students at one state university asked how many hours they slept on nights before exams. Most reported fewer than six hours, and about one in four reported fewer than four. Students who slept fewer than six hours were also more likely to report feeling anxious during the exam. The survey did not record exam scores. The university's counseling center has since added a workshop on planning study time, which it advertises during the first week of each semester.

Which statement goes beyond what the passage supports?
o: Short sleep before exams was linked to anxiety among students surveyed.
Students who slept fewer than six hours earned lower exam scores.
The counseling center now offers a workshop on planning study time.
Most of the students surveyed slept fewer than six hours before exams.
w: The passage says outright that the survey did not record exam scores, so no conclusion about scores can be drawn. The other three statements restate or directly follow from the passage.

n.0: Supported: students sleeping under six hours were more likely to report anxiety, which is a link, not a cause.
n.2: Supported: the passage says the counseling center added this workshop.
n.3: Supported: the passage says most students reported fewer than six hours.

q:
Read the passage.

The Oak Street Clinic now opens at 7 a.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays, an hour earlier than before. The change followed a survey in which many patients said they could not keep daytime appointments without missing work. Since the change, the clinic's early slots have been booked weeks in advance, while its 2 p.m. slots often go unfilled. The clinic's director says she is considering adding early hours on Mondays as well, but she has not yet set a date or hired extra staff.

Which statement is an inference supported by the passage rather than a fact stated in it?
o: The clinic now opens an hour earlier than before on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
The clinic will begin opening early on Mondays starting next month.
Many of the clinic's patients find early slots easier to keep than midday ones.
The clinic's director is considering adding early hours on Mondays as well.
w: The passage never says patients prefer early slots, but the evidence supports it: early slots are booked weeks ahead, 2 p.m. slots go unfilled, and patients reported trouble attending without missing work. Combining those details is an inference.

n.0: This is stated directly in the first sentence, so it is a located fact, not an inference.
n.1: Goes beyond the passage: the director has not set a date or hired staff.
n.3: This is stated directly in the passage, so it is not an inference.

q:
Read the passage.

Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium. The skin makes vitamin D when it is exposed to sunlight, but people who live far from the equator make much less of it in winter, when the sun stays low in the sky. A survey in one northern state found that more residents had low vitamin D levels in February than in August. Few foods contain much vitamin D naturally; fatty fish and egg yolks are two exceptions. Many brands of milk and breakfast cereal have vitamin D added during processing.

Based on the passage, which statement is supported?
o: People in northern states should take vitamin D supplements throughout the winter.
Low vitamin D was more common in the surveyed state in late winter than in late summer.
Milk is one of the best natural sources of vitamin D for most people in the country.
A lack of vitamin D causes the bones of adults to soften and weaken over time.
w: The passage reports that more residents of the northern state had low levels in February (late winter) than in August (late summer), which matches the explanation about weaker winter sunlight.

n.0: A recommendation the passage never makes.
n.2: Distortion: the passage says vitamin D is added to milk, so milk is not a natural source.
n.3: Outside knowledge: the passage says vitamin D helps absorb calcium but says nothing about bones softening.

q:
Read the passage.

When the city of Linden widened Route 9 from two lanes to four, planners expected rush-hour jams to disappear. Within three years, however, delays were nearly as long as before. Traffic counts showed that many more cars now used the road. Surveys found that some drivers had switched to Route 9 from other roads, others now drove at rush hour instead of earlier or later, and some families had moved to new subdivisions built along the wider road. Researchers call this pattern induced demand: adding road space can attract enough new traffic to fill it.

Which statement accurately reflects the cause-and-effect relationship described in the passage?
o: Drivers avoided Route 9 after the widening because construction made it slower.
Longer rush-hour delays caused families to move away from the Route 9 corridor.
Widening Route 9 attracted more drivers, which brought rush-hour delays back.
New subdivisions along Route 9 brought more drivers, so the city widened it.
w: The order in the passage is: the road was widened, more drivers began using it (switching roads, changing times, moving nearby), and delays returned. The widening is the cause and the added traffic and delays are the effects.

n.0: Contradicted: traffic counts show many more cars used Route 9 after the widening.
n.1: Opposite: families moved to new subdivisions along the road, not away from it.
n.3: Reverses cause and effect: the subdivisions were built along the wider road, after the widening.

q:
Read the passage.

At Juniper Elementary, the school garden began as four raised beds behind the gym. Third graders now plant lettuce, carrots and peas each spring, and the cafeteria serves the harvest at a salad bar one week each May. Teacher Rosa Lin, who started the garden, says that students who once refused anything green now ask for second helpings of the salad they grew. Last year, the parent group raised money to add eight more beds and a rain barrel. The principal has asked other teachers whether they would like to use the garden for science lessons.

Which statements are supported by the passage? Select all that apply.
o: The cafeteria serves vegetables from the garden throughout the spring.
Several other teachers now use the garden for their science lessons.
The garden has grown larger since it was first started.
The principal is interested in expanding how the garden is used.
The parent group paid for the original four raised beds.
According to Ms. Lin, some students eat more vegetables they grew.
w: The garden went from four beds to twelve. Ms. Lin reports students asking for seconds of the salad they grew. The principal asking other teachers about science lessons shows interest in wider use.

n.0: Distortion: the harvest is served at a salad bar one week each May, not throughout the spring.
n.1: Goes beyond the passage: the principal has asked teachers whether they would like to use it; nothing says any of them do yet.
n.4: Wrong detail: the parent group paid for the eight added beds and a rain barrel, not the original four.

q:
Read the guidelines.

Volunteer Guidelines, Harbor Food Bank
Every new volunteer attends a one-hour orientation before working a first shift. After orientation, volunteers receive a login that lets them sign up for shifts online. Volunteers who wish to drive the delivery van must also show a valid driver's license to the warehouse manager and watch a twenty-minute road-safety video. Van drivers must be at least 21 years old. Shifts that involve lifting boxes heavier than 30 pounds are marked with a star on the online calendar.

Sam has just used his login to sign up online for a starred Saturday shift.

Based on the guidelines, which statement about Sam must be true?
o: Sam is at least 21 years old and has a valid driver's license.
Sam will drive the delivery van during Saturday's shift.
Sam has watched the twenty-minute road-safety video.
Sam has already completed the volunteer orientation.
w: Volunteers receive a login after orientation, and Sam used his login to sign up. So he must have completed orientation. The star tells us only that the shift involves heavy lifting.

n.0: The age and license rules apply to van drivers, and nothing says Sam is driving.
n.1: A starred shift means heavy lifting, not driving; nothing says Sam will drive.
n.2: The video is required for van drivers; Sam has signed up for a lifting shift.

q:
Read the passage.

A local news site asked its readers to vote in an online poll: "Should the town build a new dog park?" Of the 640 readers who voted, 81 percent said yes. The site published the result under the headline "Town Wants Dog Park." The poll was open for two days, and readers could vote more than once by using different devices. The town has about 22,000 residents, and the council has not yet discussed the idea.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Most poll voters favored a dog park, but the poll may not reflect the town.
The news site changed the poll's results to support building a dog park.
Most of the town's 22,000 residents want the town to build a new dog park.
The poll shows that a new dog park would be used by most of the residents.
w: The poll shows that 81 percent of its voters said yes. But only 640 people voted in a town of about 22,000, voters chose themselves, and some could vote more than once, so the result may not represent the whole town.

n.1: Unsupported accusation: nothing suggests the site altered results.
n.2: Overgeneralizes from 640 self-selected voters to 22,000 residents, which is the error in the site's headline.
n.3: Goes beyond the evidence: a poll about building a park says nothing about how many people would use it.

q:
Read the passage.

A city health report found that neighborhoods with more fast-food restaurants per block also had higher rates of diabetes. The same neighborhoods had fewer full-service grocery stores, lower average incomes and fewer parks than other parts of the city. The report's authors noted that their data showed only where these features occurred together, not which ones, if any, caused the others. They recommended a follow-up study that would track the same residents over several years.

Which statement is best supported by the report as described?
o: Residents of these neighborhoods prefer fast food to meals that they cook at home.
Closing fast-food restaurants would lower the city's rate of diabetes.
Diabetes is more common where several features cluster, but the cause is unclear.
Fast-food restaurants are the main cause of diabetes in these neighborhoods.
w: The report found that several features (fast food, fewer groceries, lower incomes, fewer parks) occur together with higher diabetes rates, and the authors state that the data do not show cause. This option keeps to that limit.

n.0: Unsupported: the report describes restaurant counts, not what residents prefer to eat.
n.1: A prediction that assumes fast food causes diabetes, which the data do not show.
n.3: Treats a correlation as a cause, which the authors explicitly warn against.

q:
Read the passage.

Every evening at six, Mr. Okafor carried a folding chair to the end of his driveway and sat facing the street until the streetlights came on. Neighbors waved, and he waved back but rarely spoke. On the day a moving truck arrived at the house across the street, he stayed out past dark. The next evening, a young woman from the new family crossed the street with a plate of cookies. Mr. Okafor stood, unfolded a second chair that had been leaning behind his own, and offered it to her.

Which inference about Mr. Okafor is best supported by the passage?
o: He sits outside each evening in order to watch for moving trucks.
He dislikes his longtime neighbors and prefers to be left alone.
He was open to company, though he rarely started conversations himself.
He has been lonely since his wife passed away a short time ago.
w: He rarely speaks first, yet he had a second chair ready and offered it as soon as someone approached. Those details support the idea that he welcomed company even though he did not seek it out.

n.0: Distortion: he sits out every evening; the moving truck appeared on one day only.
n.1: Contradicted: he waves back at neighbors and offers the visitor a chair.
n.3: An assumption: the passage never mentions a wife or any loss.

q:
Read the passage.

In January, Lakeside Clinic launched a phone app that sends patients appointment reminders. Missed appointments fell from 18 percent in December to 11 percent in March. In February, the clinic also began calling every patient the day before a visit, and it moved its Monday appointments, historically the most often missed, to later in the morning. The clinic manager praised the app in the staff newsletter.

A reader concludes that the app alone caused missed appointments to fall. Which detail from the passage shows that this conclusion goes beyond the evidence?
o: The clinic also began calling every patient the day before.
Missed appointments fell from 18 percent to 11 percent by March.
The clinic launched its reminder app in January of that year.
The app sends patients reminders before their appointments.
w: The phone calls began during the same period the drop occurred, so they are another possible cause. A conclusion that the app alone was responsible ignores this competing explanation.

n.1: The size of the drop shows that something worked, not which change caused it.
n.2: The launch date fits the app being a cause; it does not show the conclusion overreaches.
n.3: Describing what the app does is consistent with the conclusion; it does not challenge it.

q:
Read the handbook section.

Volunteer Handbook, Section 4: Patient Escort
As you practiced during orientation, lock both wheels of a wheelchair before a patient sits down or stands up. Use the service elevators near the cafeteria rather than the public elevators in the main lobby, which are often crowded during visiting hours. Volunteers do not move patients on stretchers or patients connected to IV pumps; ask the unit clerk to page transport staff instead. If a patient says they feel faint, stop, lock the wheels and call for help using the nearest staff phone.

Which assumption about its readers does the handbook's author most clearly make?
o: Readers have worked as transport staff at other hospitals.
Readers know how to operate IV pumps safely on their own.
Readers have already attended an orientation session.
Readers usually work their shifts during visiting hours.
w: The phrase "As you practiced during orientation" shows the author expects readers to have attended orientation already.

n.0: Unsupported: readers are told to ask for transport staff, which suggests they are not transport staff.
n.1: Contradicted: volunteers are told not to move patients connected to IV pumps.
n.3: Unsupported: visiting hours are mentioned only to explain why the lobby elevators are crowded.

q:
Read the directions.

Directions for Use
Take one tablet by mouth every 12 hours, with food. Swallow the tablet whole; do not crush or chew it. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if your next dose is due in less than 4 hours, skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the usual time. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed dose. Store at room temperature, away from moisture.

Jordan takes his doses at 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. At 5 p.m., he realizes that he forgot his 8 a.m. dose.

According to the directions, what should Jordan do?
o: Take the missed dose now with food, then take his next dose at 8 p.m.
Take two tablets with food at 8 p.m. to make up for the missed dose.
Skip the missed dose and take his next dose at 8 p.m. as usual.
Take the missed dose now and move his next dose to 5 a.m. tomorrow.
w: At 5 p.m., Jordan's next dose (8 p.m.) is due in 3 hours, which is less than 4. The "However" exception applies: skip the missed dose and take the next one at the usual time.

n.0: Follows the general rule but misses the exception: with the next dose only 3 hours away, the missed dose is skipped.
n.1: The directions forbid taking two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
n.3: The directions never say to shift the schedule; with the next dose under 4 hours away, the missed dose is skipped.

q:
Read the directions.

Testing Your Well Water for Bacteria
1. Wash your hands. Do not touch the inside of the bottle or cap.
2. Remove the aerator (screen) from the end of the kitchen faucet.
3. Run cold water for 5 minutes.
4. Before filling, check that the white powder is still inside the bottle. Do not rinse it out.
5. Fill the bottle to the 100 mL line, not to the top.
6. Cap tightly and write the date and time of collection on the label.
7. Keep the sample cold and deliver it to the lab within 24 hours.

What are the symptoms? The most common first sign is cramping of the jaw muscles, which is why tetanus is sometimes called lockjaw. Painful muscle stiffness can then spread through the body.
How can I prevent it? Adults need a tetanus booster every 10 years. If you get a deep or dirty wound and your last booster was more than 5 years ago, a doctor may recommend a booster right away.

According to the passage, when might a doctor recommend a tetanus booster sooner than the usual 10 years?
o: When a person with a dirty wound had a booster over 5 years ago
When a person has spent time with someone who has tetanus
When a person regularly works with soil, dust or animal manure
When a person begins to feel cramping in the muscles of the jaw
w: Under "How can I prevent it?" the passage says that after a deep or dirty wound, a doctor may recommend a booster right away if the last one was more than 5 years ago.

n.1: Contradicted: the passage says tetanus is not spread from person to person.
n.2: Soil, dust and manure are where spores live; the passage does not link working with them to an early booster.
n.3: Jaw cramping is listed under symptoms as a first sign of the illness, not as a reason for an early booster.

q:

46 years
11 years
29 years
